# `deploy/compose/tls`

Certificate material for the tunnel gateway and for the two authorities the
connector has to trust.

**Nothing in this directory is committed.** It is generated by the end-to-end
scripts on the machine that runs the scenario, and it is key material for
throwaway authorities that exist for the duration of a test.

## What lands here

| File | Written by | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `tunnel-ca.pem` | `./configure` | nothing directly; signs `gateway.crt` and is bundled into `connector-trust.pem` |
| `gateway.crt` | `./configure` | `REVIEWPLANE_TUNNEL_TLS_CERT_FILE` |
| `gateway.key` | `./configure` | `REVIEWPLANE_TUNNEL_TLS_KEY_FILE` |
| `connector-ca.pem` | `e2e/run.sh` | `REVIEWPLANE_TUNNEL_CONNECTOR_CA_FILE` |
| `connector-trust.pem` | `e2e/run.sh` | `REVIEWPLANE_CONTROL_PLANE_CA_FILE` |

There are **two** authorities here, and keeping them apart is the point.

- **The tunnel CA** (`tunnel-ca.pem`) is generated locally before anything
  starts, and issues the gateway's leaf. It is a real CA rather than a
  self-signed leaf because Go refuses a self-signed leaf presented as a trust
  anchor — `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` — which is what the
  connector's data channel hits otherwise. The browser worker does not use this
  chain at all: it pins the leaf's public key (ADR-0015), and
  `./configure` writes that pin to `.env` as
  `REVIEWPLANE_TUNNEL_CERTIFICATE_SPKI`.
- **The connector CA** (`connector-ca.pem`) is **exported from the running
  control plane**, which owns the authority that issues connector identities. It
  cannot exist before the control plane does, so `run.sh` fetches it from
  `GET /api/v1/connectors/certificate-authority` and recreates the gateway with
  it in place. That is why the gateway restarts partway through the scenario.

`connector-trust.pem` is the two concatenated. The connector makes outbound TLS
connections to two different peers — the control plane, which serves a
certificate from the connector CA, and the gateway, which serves one from the
tunnel CA — so its trust store holds both anchors. A bundle rather than a wider
setting: each anchor is named, and neither peer can present a certificate the
other's authority signed.

The gateway refuses to start unless all three of its settings name a readable
file (`services/tunnel-gateway/cmd/tunnel-gateway/main.go`), so a missing
certificate is a startup failure with a named setting rather than a listener
that quietly comes up without mutual TLS.

## Permissions

This directory is mounted read-only at `/etc/reviewplane/tls` in the gateway and
in the `dev-fixture` container, both of which run as uid 10001. A file-based
mount keeps the host's ownership, and Compose ignores `uid`/`gid`/`mode` outside
Swarm, so anything a container must read is mode 0644 rather than 0600 — the
directory not being shared is what protects it, not the file mode.

The tunnel CA's private key is **not** in this directory. It is written to
`deploy/compose/ca/tunnel-ca.key` (0600, in a 0700 directory), which is mounted
into nothing. Nothing in either container needs it — a CA key signs
certificates, and signing happens on the host — so it has no business being
reachable from inside one. Its mode already denies both service users, but
"unreadable material inside a mount" is a weaker property than "material that is
not in the mount", and only the second survives someone later loosening a mode
or adding a container that runs as root.

Do not copy this arrangement outside a test deployment.

## Why `*.internal.invalid`

A browser reaches a published service at
`https://<public_alias>.internal.invalid/`
(`services/tunnel-gateway/README.md`). The serving certificate therefore needs a
subject alternative name covering `*.internal.invalid`, because the alias is
allocated per published service and is not known when the certificate is made.

`.invalid` is reserved by RFC 6761 and is guaranteed never to resolve in the
public DNS. That is the point: the internal origin cannot be confused with a
real name, and a certificate for it is worthless outside this deployment.

The leaf's SAN covers more than the wildcard, because the gateway is dialled by
different names by different peers: `*.internal.invalid` and `internal.invalid`
by the browser worker, `tunnel-gateway` by the control plane and the connector,
and `localhost`/`127.0.0.1` for a direct local dial. A name missing from the SAN
fails verification at that one peer, which reads as that component being broken
rather than as a certificate problem — so the SAN is deliberately wider than any
single caller needs.

## Generating it

```bash
deploy/compose/configure                 # tunnel-ca.*, gateway.crt, gateway.key
deploy/compose/e2e/run.sh                 # connector-ca.pem, connector-trust.pem
```

`./configure` leaves an existing certificate alone; pass `--force` to
replace the whole set. Regenerate rather than reuse across machines: these are
test certificates, and a long-lived private key sitting in a working tree is the
thing this directory is set up to prevent.

Do not hand-generate `connector-ca.pem`. The gateway verifies connector client
certificates against it, so it has to be the authority the control plane is
actually issuing from; a locally invented one produces a mutual-TLS handshake
failure at the point a connector opens its data channel, which is a long way
from the cause.

Regenerating `tunnel-ca.pem` invalidates `connector-trust.pem`, because the
bundle holds a copy rather than a reference. Re-run `run.sh` rather than
replacing the CA underneath a bundle that still names the old one.

## Version control

`.gitignore` at the repository root carries the entry that keeps this directory
empty of key material, so the only tracked files here are this README and
`.gitkeep`:

```gitignore
deploy/compose/tls/*
!deploy/compose/tls/.gitkeep
!deploy/compose/tls/README.md
```

Every generated file above is covered by it. If a file is added here that must
be tracked, it needs its own negation; nothing else should be.

If a key is ever committed, rotating it is not optional and deleting the commit
is not sufficient: treat it as disclosed, regenerate the authority, and reissue
every certificate it signed.
